title: How To Handle A Disruptive Autistic Student
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to recurring reader questions, Linsin -- explicitly disclaiming any special-education credential and speaking only as a classroom teacher -- lays out a nine-point general approach to autistic students in regular classrooms who struggle to follow standard rules. His sequence starts with giving every student, including autistic students, the same initial opportunity to learn the classroom management plan, then trusting the overall classroom climate created by good whole-class management (rather than individual interventions) to shape behavior most effectively. Where a student genuinely cannot yet meet a standard expectation, he recommends adjusting the plan collaboratively with the student and their parents (for example, additional warnings or reduced time-out length), while emphasizing that minor disruptions in an otherwise well-managed, on-task classroom often don't need to be addressed at all -- the rest of the class can absorb and accept a difference without it undermining consistency. For dangerous behavior he draws a hard line, requiring immediate escalation to administration, parent contact, and documentation, and closes with unusually direct advice for teachers being left unsupported by their administration: consider changing schools if safety can't be assured.
points: Give autistic students the same initial opportunity to learn the classroom management plan as everyone else, rather than assuming exceptions from the start.
Trust the overall classroom climate created by excellent whole-class management to shape behavior more than any individual, targeted intervention.
When a student genuinely can't meet an expectation yet, adjust the plan collaboratively with the student and parents (e.g., extra warnings, shortened time-out) rather than abandoning structure.
Minor disruptions in an otherwise well-managed, on-task class often don't need direct correction at all -- classmates can accept the difference without consistency breaking down.
For dangerous behavior, escalate immediately to administration with documentation and parent contact every time, and consider changing schools if safety can't be assured.
quotes: I’m not an expert in autism. Nor do I have a degree or teaching credential in special education. I write only from the perspective of a classroom teacher.
I believe that the SCM approach—with its focus on responsibility, intrinsic motivation, pursuit of excellence, and kindness and respect—is best for all students.
It’s not you and your individual interventions that make the difference. It’s the SCM classroom climate and culture itself that is most impactful and best helps each student improve.

An autistic student only disrupts the class if you and your students are disrupted. In other words, as long as the class is well-behaved and on-task, then a calling out or other noise is just that. Keep teaching. Let it go. It’s okay and your class will understand.

If the student continues to act dangerously—running out of the room, climbing on cabinets, hitting others, etc.—then you must call for help, document the behavior, and then seek direction from your principal.

If your administration ignores you and you’re being hung out to dry, then you should consider changing schools. Really. If you can’t ensure your own safety and that of your students, then you need to get out of there.
The overarching answer to autistic students who may not be able to follow rules is compassion combined with excellent all-class classroom management. It can do wonders when applied day after day.
